script.opening: "So… I said I wanted some antidepressants to feel better, and I have been a bit down. But honestly, that’s not really why I’m here. It’s… god, this is embarrassing… I finish way too quickly when I’m with my girlfriend, almost straight away, and it’s killing my confidence and causing arguments. I didn’t know how to bring it up."

facts.text: Ejaculates "almost straight away" — within about a minute of penetration, nearly every time. Feels no control. "It’s been a problem for a while" — if pressed, since his first relationship at 18, so always. Masturbation alone lasts longer.
"They’re fine. It’s just the finishing." Morning erections normal. No pain, no discharge, no pain on ejaculation. No urinary symptoms.

A bit low for a couple of months, "mostly because of this". Sleeping and eating OK, still enjoys football and gaming. Worries about it constantly. No thoughts of self-harm or suicide. Some anxiety before sex.
Girlfriend, Priya, for 18 months. They argue about it; she said "it’s like you don’t care about me". He hasn’t told her he was coming today.
Fit. No medicines, no recreational drugs. No thyroid symptoms. Alcohol at weekends, about 12 units. Non-smoker. No allergies. No fainting or dizziness on standing. No heart problems.
Works in IT support. Lives with two flatmates.

Start by talking about feeling down and asking for antidepressants. Disclose the real problem in the opening but hesitantly; if the doctor responds awkwardly or moves straight to depression, go quiet and accept an antidepressant. If the doctor is relaxed and non-judgemental, open up. Prefer to try techniques and a spray first.

ice.ideas: "I thought maybe antidepressants — I read somewhere they can help with this."
ice.concerns: HIDDEN AGENDA — "I’m worried she’ll leave me, and I just want to feel normal." Embarrassed and afraid there is something physically wrong.

cues: "That’s not really why I’m here" — the hidden agenda; the stated reason was cover.
"It’s killing my confidence" — psychological impact and mood.
"I haven’t told her I was coming" — involving his partner in treatment.

checkpoints.text: Elicits the HIDDEN AGENDA sensitively — creating safety, picking up the hesitancy and inviting the real concern — rather than simply prescribing an antidepressant for "low mood"

Defines and CLASSIFIES premature ejaculation (lifelong: within about 1 minute; acquired: often about 3 minutes or less — ISSM), recognising acquired PE warrants seeking a cause (ED, anxiety/relationship, prostatitis, thyroid, drugs)
Screens the PSYCHOLOGICAL/relationship context — anxiety (performance), low mood (explores/treats a genuine depression and asks about self-harm, NICE NG222), and partner/relationship impact

Checks for coexisting ERECTILE DYSFUNCTION (treat first if present) and considers basic checks (e.g. TFTs) in acquired PE, offering a face-to-face genital examination and blood pressure check, with consent and a chaperone, where indicated

Offers EVIDENCE-BASED treatment — behavioural techniques (stop-start/squeeze), topical anaesthetics, and an SSRI (dapoxetine on-demand with its safety points — orthostatic check, syncope, no alcohol, no other SSRI, ages 18–64, once in 24 hours — or off-label daily) — with partner involvement and psychosexual referral if refractory
Handles an embarrassing topic with destigmatising empathy, validates the impact on confidence/relationship, and checks understanding
Negotiates a treatment plan he is comfortable starting (behavioural, topical or tablet), framing it as a positive and solvable issue and inviting his preference and partner involvement

Reaches a supportive plan: PE classified, ED addressed, mood/anxiety managed, treatment options offered with follow-up in about four weeks (mood re-screened)/psychosexual referral — the real issue treated, not an antidepressant for "feeling low"

worked.txt: "Thank you for telling me what’s really going on — that took courage, and there’s absolutely nothing to be embarrassed about. This is really common and very treatable. Let’s sort it out together."

"Has it always been this way, or is it newer? … If it’s changed recently I’d look for a reason. And how are your erections — firm enough? Sometimes rushing because you’re worried about losing the erection drives this, and we’d treat that first."
"You mentioned feeling a bit down — how much of that is the worry about this? Performance anxiety feeds the problem, and if there’s a genuine low mood underneath we’ll treat that too."

"There are techniques that genuinely help — the ‘stop-start’ and ‘squeeze’ methods — which I’ll explain, and doing them with your girlfriend helps. There’s also a numbing spray for the tip of the penis a few minutes before sex — wipe off any excess so your girlfriend doesn’t feel numb."

"And there’s an effective tablet — a type of antidepressant called dapoxetine taken one to three hours before sex, no more than once a day, or a daily one — that delays things. It can cause dizziness or fainting, so I’d check your blood pressure standing up first, and you’d avoid alcohol with it. So ironically an ‘antidepressant’ may help, but for the right reason."

"If it’s not settling, or there’s a lot tied up in the relationship, a psychosexual therapist is excellent. Bring your girlfriend along if she’s willing — this is a team effort, and it really does improve. Let’s review in about four weeks, and if your mood gets worse or you have any thoughts of harming yourself, contact us straight away."

f.learning: A young man presenting "for antidepressants to feel better" may be masking an embarrassing sexual concern — here PREMATURE EJACULATION (PE) — so the first skill is eliciting the HIDDEN AGENDA sensitively, creating safety and inviting the real issue rather than prescribing an antidepressant for "low mood" and missing it. PE (ISSM definition, international) is ejaculation that always or nearly always occurs within about 1 minute of penetration in LIFELONG PE, or after a bothersome reduction in latency, often to about 3 minutes or less, in ACQUIRED PE, with a lack of control and DISTRESS (EAU also describes variable and subjective PE, managed with reassurance); classify LIFELONG versus ACQUIRED, as acquired PE warrants seeking a cause (erectile dysfunction, performance anxiety/relationship factors, prostatitis, thyroid dysfunction, drugs). Screen the psychological and relationship context (anxiety, low mood — exploring/treating genuine depression — and partner impact), and crucially check for coexisting ERECTILE DYSFUNCTION, which commonly accompanies PE and should generally be treated first (rushing to ejaculate before losing the erection can drive PE), with basic checks such as TFTs where indicated, a face-to-face genital examination and blood pressure check, with consent and a chaperone offered, where indicated, and a proper depression assessment including self-harm risk (NICE NG222). Offer evidence-based treatment: behavioural/psychosexual techniques (stop-start and squeeze), self-help and partner involvement; topical anaesthetics (lidocaine with prilocaine spray, licensed for lifelong PE; creams such as EMLA off-label; wipe off excess to protect the partner); and pharmacotherapy — an SSRI delays ejaculation (dapoxetine on-demand, licensed for PE in men aged 18–64, 30 mg 1–3 hours before sex, no more than once in 24 hours, after an orthostatic check, without alcohol or another SSRI/serotonergic drug; or off-label daily SSRIs; BNF) — with psychosexual referral for refractory cases or significant relationship/psychological factors. The skill is the empathic hidden-agenda elicitation, classification, ED check and offering effective, destigmatised treatment (EAU 2024, international; ISSM 2014; BNF; NICE NG222; BSSM 2018).

knowledge.guideline: [1] EAU Guidelines on Sexual and Reproductive Health (Limited Update March 2026, international) · [2] ISSM definition of premature ejaculation, Serefoglu et al., J Sex Med 2014 (international) · [3] NICE NG222 Depression in adults (2022, updated December 2025) · [4] BSSM guidelines on the management of erectile dysfunction (Hackett et al., 2018)
knowledge.summary: A request for antidepressants can hide a sexual problem. Here the real agenda is premature ejaculation causing distress and relationship strain. Make it safe to talk, then confirm PE against the ISSM definition, classify lifelong versus acquired (acquired needs a cause looked for), and check for erectile dysfunction, which is treated first if present. Screen mood properly rather than prescribing for ‘feeling low’. Offer behavioural techniques, a topical anaesthetic spray and, if wanted, on-demand dapoxetine or an off-label daily SSRI, with partner involvement and psychosexual therapy where relationship or anxiety factors dominate.

points.t: ISSM [2]: lifelong PE is ejaculation that always or nearly always occurs before or within about 1 minute of vaginal penetration; acquired PE is a clinically significant, bothersome reduction in latency, often to about 3 minutes or less. Both need an inability to delay on all or nearly all occasions and negative personal consequences such as distress or avoidance. The EAU [1] also describes variable and subjective PE, which are managed mainly with reassurance and education.

Look for a cause [1]: erectile dysfunction, performance anxiety or relationship problems, prostatitis, hyperthyroidism, and drug use or withdrawal. Treat the cause first. A genital examination is only needed if the history suggests a physical cause, and is arranged face to face with a chaperone; check blood pressure (a home or pharmacy reading is fine); thyroid function where features suggest it.
ED commonly coexists. Rushing to ejaculate for fear of losing the erection can drive PE, so treat ED first with a PDE5 inhibitor and cardiovascular risk assessment [1,4]; PE may then improve.

He booked for antidepressants. Assess depression properly (NG222 [3]), including risk. If he has depression needing an SSRI, a daily SSRI may also delay ejaculation; dapoxetine must not be combined with another SSRI or serotonergic drug.

Behavioural techniques (stop-start, squeeze) with his partner, and psychosexual therapy for anxiety or relationship factors; combining behavioural and drug treatment may be more effective than either alone [1]. Topical lidocaine with prilocaine spray, licensed for lifelong PE, applied before intercourse, dose per BNF; excess is wiped off to avoid numbness in the partner. Dapoxetine, licensed for men aged 18–64: 30 mg 1–3 hours before sex, no more than once in 24 hours; check for orthostatic hypotension first, avoid alcohol, and do not combine with a PDE5 inhibitor in routine primary care. Daily SSRIs are off-label.
Review response and side effects within weeks; re-screen mood; refer to psychosexual services if treatment fails or relationship factors dominate.

model.text: Hello Mr Anand, I’m Dr Evans. What can I do for you today?

So… I said I wanted some antidepressants to feel better, and I have been a bit down. But honestly, that’s not really why I’m here. It’s… this is embarrassing. I finish way too quickly when I’m with my girlfriend, almost straight away, and it’s killing my confidence and causing arguments. I didn’t know how to bring it up.

Thank you for telling me. That took courage, and it’s something doctors help with often. It’s common and it’s treatable. Shall we look at it properly, and I’ll come back to how you’ve been feeling in yourself too?
Yes. Thanks.
When you say straight away, roughly how long is it from penetration until you ejaculate? And does it happen every time?
Almost straight away. Nearly every time.
Has it always been this way since you first had sex, or is it a change from how things used to be?
I’m not sure. It’s been a problem for a while.
That’s fine. It helps to know because if it has changed, we look for a cause. How are your erections: firm enough, and do they last?
They’re fine. It’s just the finishing.
Any pain in the pelvis or when ejaculating, burning when you pass urine, or discharge? Any weight loss, shaking, palpitations or feeling hot all the time?
model.why: Prostatitis and hyperthyroidism as causes of acquired PE

model.text: No, none of that.
Any medicines, recreational drugs or alcohol that I should know about?
Nothing really.
You said you’ve been a bit down. How much of that is this problem, and how much is there on its own? How are sleep, energy and enjoyment? Have you had any thoughts of harming yourself?
It’s mostly this. I’m worried about it all the time. No, nothing like harming myself.
How is it affecting things with your girlfriend? Does she know you’re here?
We argue about it. I haven’t told her I was coming.
What were you hoping I could do? And what worries you most?
I thought maybe tablets. I’m worried she’ll leave, and I just want to feel normal.

Nothing you’ve told me suggests a physical cause, so I don’t think you need an examination today. If anything changes, I can see you in person with a chaperone. Could you get your blood pressure checked at the pharmacy this week?
model.why: Explains why an examination isn’t needed; offers in-person exam with chaperone if indicated

model.text: Your blood pressure reading on your record is normal too.

This is premature ejaculation. It’s one of the commonest sexual problems in men. Anxiety makes it worse, and it makes anxiety worse, which is the cycle you’re in. The low mood sounds mainly driven by this, so I don’t think a daily antidepressant just for feeling low is the answer today.
model.why: Names the diagnosis; addresses the stated request honestly

model.text: There are three kinds of help, and they work best together. First, techniques: the stop-start and squeeze methods, ideally practised with your girlfriend. I’ll give you written instructions. Second, a numbing spray for the tip of the penis a few minutes before sex; wipe off any excess so she doesn’t feel numb.

Third, a tablet called dapoxetine, taken one to three hours before sex. It’s related to antidepressants but short-acting and made for this. It can cause dizziness or fainting, so I’d check your blood pressure standing up, and you’d avoid alcohol with it. Some men take a daily antidepressant instead, which is off-licence.
model.why: Dapoxetine with safety checks; daily SSRI off-label

model.text: I think I’ll try the techniques and the spray first. Maybe the tablet later.

That’s a sensible start. If the worry or the relationship tension is a big part of it, a psychosexual therapist can help you both. Would you consider telling your girlfriend? It often takes the pressure off.
model.why: Respects his choice; psychosexual therapy; partner involvement

model.text: Yes. I think it would help if she knew it’s a medical thing.

Let’s review in about four weeks to see how it’s going and check your mood again. If your mood gets worse, or you have any thoughts of harming yourself, contact us straight away. What will you take away from today?
It’s common and treatable. Stop-start and squeeze, the spray before sex, maybe the tablet later, talk to my girlfriend, and come back in a month.
That’s it. Well done for bringing it up.

social.t: PE commonly causes relationship strain. Involving the partner improves outcomes and reduces blame.
Performance anxiety can generalise to avoidance of intimacy and low self-esteem.

legal.t: GMC guidance on intimate examinations and chaperones: explain why the examination is needed, get consent, and offer a chaperone, recording the discussion.

professional.t: Patients often present a more acceptable reason first. Responding to cues rather than the stated request is core consulting skill.
Daily SSRIs for PE are off-label: explain this and record the discussion.

community.t: NHS psychosexual services and accredited sexual and relationship therapists offer couple or individual work.

redFlags: Pelvic pain, dysuria or discharge: prostatitis or STI

playbook.diagnosisLay: “Ejaculation is a reflex. When you’re anxious, the reflex fires sooner, which makes you more anxious next time. The techniques, spray and tablet all help retrain or slow that reflex.”

items.fix: Respond to his hesitancy and invite the real issue.
Normalise, use plain language and take a matter-of-fact history.

items.why: ED is common, drives PE and is treated first.
items.fix: Ask directly and treat ED first if present.

items.why: Acquired PE needs a cause looked for.
items.fix: Ask when it started; screen prostatitis, thyroid and drugs.

items.why: Syncope risk; interaction with SSRIs; alcohol.
items.fix: Orthostatic check, BNF dosing, no other serotonergic drugs, avoid alcohol.

items.why: He reported low mood; risk must be reviewed.
items.fix: Screen risk now and review in about four weeks.

Premature ejaculation named, with the anxiety cycle explained.
Behavioural techniques, topical spray, dapoxetine with orthostatic and alcohol advice; his choice respected.
No SSRI for ‘feeling low’ without depression; interaction rule with other SSRIs; psychosexual therapy and partner involvement.
Review in about four weeks; mood safety-net; teach-back.

social.t: PE commonly causes relationship strain. Involving the partner improves outcomes and reduces blame.
Performance anxiety can generalise to avoidance of intimacy and low self-esteem.

legal.t: GMC guidance on intimate examinations and chaperones: explain why the examination is needed, get consent, and offer a chaperone, recording the discussion.

professional.t: Patients often present a more acceptable reason first. Responding to cues rather than the stated request is core consulting skill.
Daily SSRIs for PE are off-label: explain this and record the discussion.

community.t: NHS psychosexual services and accredited sexual and relationship therapists offer couple or individual work.

redFlags: Pelvic pain, dysuria or discharge: prostatitis or STI
ice: Concern: girlfriend may leave; feeling abnormal

SCA_PLAYBOOK.diagnosis: “This is premature ejaculation, and anxiety about it is keeping the problem going.”
SCA_PLAYBOOK.diagnosisLay: “Ejaculation is a reflex. When you’re anxious, the reflex fires sooner, which makes you more anxious next time. The techniques, spray and tablet all help retrain or slow that reflex.”

management.reflectIce: “You came asking for antidepressants. What you really need is treatment for this, and I think your mood will lift with it.”
management.psychosocial: Encourage partner involvement; psychosexual therapy if anxiety or relationship factors dominate.
sharedPlan: Stop-start and squeeze techniques with written instructions
Topical lidocaine with prilocaine spray, dose per BNF
Dapoxetine 30 mg 1–3 hours before sex if chosen, after orthostatic check; no alcohol
Psychosexual therapy; review in about four weeks
safetyNet: Worsening mood or thoughts of self-harm: contact the practice urgently
Dizziness or fainting with dapoxetine: stop and seek review

SCA_PITFALLS.intro: The case hinges on the hidden agenda. Marks go to picking up the cue, classifying PE, checking for ED and mood, and offering real treatment instead of an antidepressant for ‘feeling low’.

items.fail: Taking the antidepressant request at face value.
items.fix: Respond to his hesitancy and invite the real issue.
Normalise, use plain language and take a matter-of-fact history.

items.why: ED is common, drives PE and is treated first.
items.fix: Ask directly and treat ED first if present.

items.why: Acquired PE needs a cause looked for.
items.fix: Ask when it started; screen prostatitis, thyroid and drugs.

items.why: Syncope risk; interaction with SSRIs; alcohol.
items.fix: Orthostatic check, BNF dosing, no other serotonergic drugs, avoid alcohol.

items.why: He reported low mood; risk must be reviewed.
items.fix: Screen risk now and review in about four weeks.
